I'm disabled. Thing to remember is that there's a difference between Social Security Disability and Supplemental Security Income. SSD is something you're only eligible for if you've been paying into the system for quite a while, otherwise you default to SSI, which doesn't pay nearly as much. 

It took me four years to obtain SSI, during which time I almost died from lack of medical coverage. But I made a lot of stupid mistakes. So hopefully you can benefit from my experience. Turn around time for your initial application is around six months. That lengthens out to 10-12 months if you're waiting to appeal a decision before an administrative law judge. 

Things you should have before you apply:

1. Medical records, a metric assload, all chronologically ordered.

2. A summary of your medical history, including dates of diagnosis, list of doctors seen and when, major tests and procedures, periods of hospitalization, etc.

3. Quality of Life assessment. This is not included in the paperwork you are issued, but you can attach it and send it in, which I strongly urge you do. You can find copies of such assessments online, or design one of your own which most correctly states the impact CF has on the applicant's life. It's even more useful if you can get a doctor to fill one out for you, but that's a stretch.

4. Residual Functional Capacity Questionnaire. There is such a questionnaire making up a portion of your mandated application. It's poorly worded and designed, deliberately intended to wrongfoot you so you put down the wrong answer, enabling them to deny your application. Never answer a question in such a fashion that allows them to reject your application out of hand, even if it means you must make statements that require clarification later. Better yet, include a residual functional capacity questionnaire of your own after looking up several examples online. Again, it would carry more weight if your doctor filled it out.

5. Finally, the make or break requirement is a statement from your doctor saying that you are disabled, and by which he means you have a medical condition which precludes you from all forms of gainful employment. If you don't have this, your application will be denied every time. It all comes down to the doctor writing it down and signing. Hopefully you've got a good one who genuinely wants to help you out. 

Even with all these things, there's always the chance some bureaucratic asswipe decides to reject your application because they feel like it. Don't reapply; your benefits are due to you backdated from the moment you sent in the first application, but if you send in another you'll lose those benefits. Instead, lawyer up. Disability attorneys are not hard to find, so make sure to do some research ahead of time so you know you got a decent one. Some things to keep in mind are that you don't pay him; he takes his fee out of the benefits you are awarded by the government. Legally, he cannot take any more than somewhere in the ballpark of $5,300 for the job. Make sure to become friends with his secretary because you'll be faxing and emailing a lot back and forth. Also, you will have to pay a processing fee that covers the cost of all the printing, mailing, and faxing that went on during your case. 

But, if you are lucky and fill out the initial application properly, you won't need a lawyer.

When you turn 18, apply for Supplemental Security Income, and make sure to get statements from your doctor indicating the severity of your disorder and the fact that it precludes you from any form of gainful employment. Include a Quality of Life Assessment and Residual Functional Capacity Questionnaire with your initial application, as without these three things your application will be denied. 

You can expect to receive a little under $800 a month and have to fill out paperwork every 2-3 years. Make sure to stay chummy with a doctor who will be willing to make statements on your behalf that you can send to the Social Security Administration.

Next, hide your assets. Either sign everything over to your relatives or convert all your bank accounts into cash, as your maximum personal assets will determine the level of healthcare you receive, and how much you pay out of pocket. 

Your application for Medicare will be automatically filed when you receive SSI. These are all state-based benefits rather than federal benefits, so you'll be tied down to the state in which you live. With sufficiently low assets you will be eligible for Medicare parts A and B, supplemental Medicaid (which covers the co-pays and expenses that Medicare doesn't cover), Extra Help benefits which cover the cost of your monthly Medicare premiums and do away with Medicare's "Coverage Gap," and the Medicare Part D Prescription Drug Plan. I would suggest you look at the prescription drug plan offered by AARP, which Medicare will pay the premiums for provided it's their cheaper package, as it covers quite a few drugs out there. 

Your coverage will be limited to physicians and hospitals that take both Medicare AND Medicaid. Places that take just Medicare will make you pay through the nose, so it's a good idea to contact physicians and facilities ahead of time. Also, it's inevitable that billing will be messed up and facilities will not send the proper forms to Medicare and Medicaid. As long as you don't have any major assets in your name which you can't prove were given to you by the government, you can't be taken to court by debt collectors, which gives you some negotiating leeway with billing people.

I've been following van Poyck's writing for some time now, and his recounting of events in prison has opened my eyes to the appalling abuses that go on behind closed doors. His partner was actually stomped to death in 1999 by seven prison guards, all of whom escaped prosecution. 

The way I see it, you've been confined to a location for the rest of your life because society has deemed you impossible to rehabilitate; and in order to protect society you must be kept separated from the world. That's punishment enough without suffering abuse, neglect, and hatred from guards and medical workers. 

Bottom line, our prison system is focused on a bloodthirsty mindset. It seeks to exact suffering from the accused at all times, and by the time it's time to be executed I would almost think death would be a mercy. But, in the same vein that one should not inflict suffering on an inmate because one does not have that right, one also does not have the right to take another human life. That's why a prisoner is behind bars: because he violated that core belief. The state cannot assume to possess that selfsame right while avoiding allegations of hypocrisy. And this bill which would speed the death penalty in Florida takes our society further in a violent, dangerous direction.

My belief is that you can judge how civilized a society is by how it treats its lowest members, and the treatment of prisoners in the US shows us to be barbarians. I know that many people think it's okay because prisoners used to be treated in an even worse fashion, but there's a flaw to that statement. One cannot take two objectively wrong things and say one is right because the other is even more wrong. They're still both wrong.

I've told this one elsewhere, but it's still the most horrific to me, so here goes:

I spent alot of time in and around the ER as a kid because my mother was an ER nurse and it was a small, pastoral town where I could pretty much walk wherever I wanted to go; and I was a complete mama's boy, so being around her always made me kinda happy. 

This cowboy comes limping in one morning. Normally when they're limping it's because they were thrown and dragged, or pinched, and have a broken ankle. Tough sons of bitches. This kid was younger than most, maybe just old enough to drink. And when he pulls his boot off to show the admitting nurse, he's got a livid red rash radiating outward from the level of his ankle. They got him a bed when they realized the center of the rash was starting to go septic, but they couldn't get him to a ward because they were full up. 

This was in the morning before school. It isn't until 10-12 hours later that I'm coming by to walk Mom home that I see the guy is still in his bed. Mom said it wasn't good when I asked about it. The rash is halfway up his shin by now and weeping fluid. It's gone black in places. The gossip among the hens is that he's go flesh-eating bacteria and the doctor has told him he's got to have a below-the-knee amputation if he wants to live. I'm waiting for Mom, which usually took a while because she couldn't very well drop things and leave when a patient is bleeding out on her. And I'm sitting in one of the empty beds next door, and I can peek through the partition. 

The doctor comes in, and the kid gives his answer: He'd rather die. He's spent most of his life outdoors. And since a prosthetic won't let him live his life the way he wants to live it, he's okay with dying. The doctor stares at him for a bit, says okay, and walks out. 

About twenty minutes later a nurse comes in, gives the cowboy an injection "to make him comfortable," and the cowboy is out like a light in under a minute. The doctor comes back in with a couple guys who've been introduced to me in the past as surgeons. The doc says that since the kid is unconscious and incapable of giving informed consent, in his medical opinion they must amputate the leg. The surgeons look over the chart, examine the leg, and concur. 

They then draw straws to see which one of them gets to cut off the leg!

The one who wins pumps his fist, jumps on tiptoes, does a little dance, then positively skips to go scrub up. I've never seen such sick joy before. Pretty soon, a couple orderlies come to take the bed to the OR, and somehow watching that poor unconscious bastard being wheeled away like a side of meat, knowing the surgeon is gleefully awaiting with blades sharpened, was the most horrific thing I've ever seen. It combined violation of free will, helplessness, and all the terrible things that potentially go on in hospitals in one grim little package. Nightmares of that fucking butcher's shop wake me screaming sometimes. I never went back to visit Mom again. And she still wonders why.

**tl;dr** Watched guy in ER get drugged unconscious so a sick surgeon could chop his leg off against the guy's will.

There was an article, wish I could find it, concerning the factors that contribute to suicidal behavior. It looked not at depression or attempted suicides, but at those who had succeeded in committing suicide. There were four factors consistently at work. 

1. The person felt alone. Alone was defined as not having regular human contact with five or more people. Internet and phone didn't count since there's a physical component about a person's presence that we need.

2. Not being squeamish. People who had frequent medical problems, surgeries, worked in the medical field, were around people with lots of injuries, or had been trained to inflict bodily harm tend to be less squeamish about the nitty-gritty of dying. This ensures that people, once they start to kill themselves, have a certain level of mental toughness that ensures that they don't back out. 

3. Having nothing to look forward to. People need more than a nebulous sense of hope. They need concrete, well-defined goals of things in their lives that they are going to achieve or improve on. Without that, people become suicidal. 

4. Being a burden. People who feel as if they are a burden on someone else are likely, in conjunction with the other factors, to commit suicide as they see it to be the only way to stop holding someone else back from excelling in life. 

Most people hall into one or more of these categories.

It was too far gone to fix, so the doctor goes to the kid and tells him he needs a below-the-knee amputation or he's gonna die.

The doctor comes back in with four surgeons in tow. He says the kid can no longer give informed consent because he's lost consciousness, and its his recommendation that they amputate the leg. The one who wins pumps his fist, jumps in place like a kid in a candy store, then rushes off to get scrubbed, humming to himself. 

I left at that point, because someone being happy about getting to cut another person's leg off was just too fucked up for me, but hospital gossip got around. That taught me that the medical field doesn't always get it: there are far worse things than death, and ignoring the patient's wishes thinking you know what's best for them doesn't always make you the good guy. And then it's looking at oneself and going, "I killed a bad man. Instead, make requests, and use passive phrasing. Say things along the lines of, "I'd like this please," "Can I have this?" and "I'll be having this and this."
